record.what_it_does: Global crypto exchange with spot, futures, margin, wallet and trading APIs.
record.auth_notes: Users create their own API keys and send them in the X-MBX-APIKEY header. Signed requests also carry a signature made with HMAC, RSA (PKCS#8) or Ed25519, and Binance recommends Ed25519. By default a key cannot TRADE. Binance Login (OAuth 2.0) for third-party apps is "only provided to close ecosystem partners now". The official remote MCP server uses its own browser consent flow ("Binance Agentic Account Access"), which is limited to an Agentic sub-account. For a multi-user toolkit, per-user API keys are the practical route.
record.access_notes: API keys cost nothing, but a user can only create them after enabling 2FA, depositing any amount to their Spot Account and completing identity verification (KYC). Spot testnet keys come from a GitHub login at testnet.binance.vision. OAuth (Binance Login) is limited to close ecosystem partners, and access goes through the business team. Binance.com is not available in some regions, such as the US, where Binance.US is a separate platform.
record.api_breadth_notes: Covers spot, margin, USD-M and COIN-M futures, options, wallet, sub-accounts, convert, staking, mining and more. That is well over 50 endpoints. Rate limits are per IP, not per API key. Official connectors exist for Python, JS, Java, Rust and Go, and there are Postman collections.
record.mcp_notes: Binance hosts an official MCP server at https://agent.binance.com/mcp/agentic, part of Binance Agent OS. It covers market data, plus trading in Spot, Margin, Convert, USDⓈ-M and COIN-M Futures inside a dedicated Agentic sub-account. It authenticates through a browser consent flow, stores no local API keys and has no withdrawal scope. The Binance Skills Hub is also official. Community servers such as the PyPI binance-mcp-server also exist.
record.blocker_notes: The API is buildable with per-user API keys. Each end user needs a KYC-verified, funded Binance account in a supported region and must paste in a key and secret, often with an IP whitelist. OAuth is partner-only, so there is no standard delegated-auth flow. Rate limits are per IP, so users would share one limit behind a shared backend. Trading actions are high-risk.
